item.text: {"verdicts":[{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0029-E001","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0029-E002","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0029-E003","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0029-E004","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0029-E005","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0029-E006","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"CPJ reported that from March 2023 AMLO repeatedly criticized Article 19, Proceso, Animal Político, Aristegui Noticias, and reporter Nayeli Roldán over coverage of alleged illegal government spyware use; he called Roldán unobjective, unprofessional, and part of bribed media, and accused Article 19 of U.S. government funding. The targeted journalists and organizations reported increased online abuse, misogynistic comments, threats, stalking, and safety concerns. CPJ also reported that Mexico was the Western Hemisphere’s deadliest country for journalists in 2022. Animal Político’s editorial director said AMLO never rectified false information about them.","notes":["The excerpt attributes the claim that the president never rectified false information to Animal Político’s editorial director, not directly to CPJ or as an independently established fact."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0029-E007","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"In September 2023 AMLO transferred control of the Mayan Train to SEDENA and had already transferred ports, airports, and rail administration to the military, while the government created military-controlled companies and infrastructure operators. The stated presidential rationale for the Mayan Train transfer was reducing corruption in public works; the article also discusses discipline and faster completion as possible reasons. Critics cited limited relevant military expertise, weak transparency and accountability, risks of concealed information and impunity, Indigenous-community disruption and militarization, and a Mayan Train cost increase from an initial $7.2 billion estimate to more than $28 billion.","notes":["The excerpt explicitly states reducing corruption as the president’s rationale; timely completion is presented as a possible alternative reason or effect, not as part of the stated rationale."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0029-E008","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0029-E009","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"Brookings described AMLO’s announced 2018–2024 security plan as combining root-cause policies, anti-corruption, human-rights protections, public-health measures, transitional justice, prison and security-sector reform, and a National Guard, but judged key elements unclear and unlikely to reduce violence quickly. It reported delayed or inadequate anti-corruption and prosecutorial appointments, refusal to support an autonomous attorney-general selection, continued military domestic law enforcement, opaque National Guard deployment logic, weak police reform, and unresolved risks around amnesty, militias, and drug-licensing enforcement. It described alternative livelihoods as a positive development and recommended emphasizing human rights and accountability.","notes":["The excerpt describes a human-rights promise and recommends human-rights protection and accountability; it does not explicitly characterize the human-rights-centered strategy itself as potentially positive."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0029-E010","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]}]}
